parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man arranges for someone to look after his pets while he is away.
script: Hello, Happy Paws Pet Sitting, Kim speaking.
Hi. I'm going away next month, and I need someone to look after my pets.
Of course. Can I take your name?
Hugo Barnes. B, A, R, N, E, S.
A dog and a rabbit. The rabbit's very easy, but the dog needs more attention.
Biscuit. B, I, S, C, U, I, T.
Lovely. When are you going away?
From the ninth of August, for six nights.
Yes, one tablet a day for his joints. He has to have it with his breakfast, otherwise it upsets his stomach.
No problem. How often does he need walking?
Twice a day. He loves the woods behind the house. But please don't let him go near the lake. He jumps in and it's very hard to get him out.
I'll make a note. Our rate is thirty-five pounds a night, which includes two walks a day and feeding both animals.
We always arrange a meeting before the booking starts, so the sitter can meet the animals and see the house. Would Sunday be convenient?

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A resident gives a talk about life in an eco-village.
script: Good afternoon, and welcome to Greenfield Eco-Village. I'm Hamid, and I've lived here since the village was founded.
It wasn't started by the council or by a charity. In 2008, a group of twelve families bought the land together and designed the village themselves.
Most of the houses are built from straw bales covered in clay plaster. People are often surprised, but straw is an excellent insulator, so the houses need very little heating.
Almost all our electricity comes from solar panels on the roofs. We considered a wind turbine, but the site isn't windy enough.
If you'd like to experience village life for a few days, you can stay in our guest cabin, which sleeps four.
Let me tell you about some of the shared spaces. In the common house, we cook and eat meals together twice a week. Anyone can join.
The workshop works as a tool library. Instead of everyone buying their own drill or ladder, residents borrow what they need.
In the orchard, we grow apples and pears, and every autumn we make our own apple juice.
Behind the houses there's a reed bed, which cleans all our waste water naturally, using plants.
In the shed by the entrance, we keep three electric cars, which residents share instead of owning their own.
And the farm shop, which is open to the public at weekends, sells vegetables and eggs produced in the village.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Bea and Sami, discuss their study on breakfast and concentration.
script: Bea, shall we go through the results of our breakfast study?
Sure. Just to remind ourselves, our question was whether eating breakfast affects students' concentration in morning lectures.
And participants recorded what they ate in a food diary on an app, every day for two weeks.
What surprised me was why people skipped breakfast. I assumed they weren't hungry, but most said they simply didn't have time.
Yes, that was unexpected. The weakness of our study, though, is that concentration was self-reported. People just rated how well they thought they'd concentrated, which isn't very reliable.
True. So for the next stage, I think we should add a short attention test at the start of the lecture.
Good idea. Let's check the figures. Forty percent of students skipped breakfast at least three times a week.
The most common breakfast was cereal, followed by toast.
Students who ate breakfast rated their concentration two points higher, on a ten-point scale.
Average sleep was six and a half hours a night, which is less than recommended.
And fifty-five percent drank coffee before their first lecture.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of the Olympic Games.
script: Today we're looking at the history of the Olympic Games, from ancient Greece to the present day.

According to tradition, the first ancient Olympic Games were held in 776 BC at Olympia, in southern Greece. They were held in honour of the god Zeus, and they were as much a religious festival as a sporting event.
Only free Greek men could compete. Women were not allowed to take part, and married women were not even allowed to watch.
Winners did not receive gold medals. Instead, they were given a crown made of olive leaves, although they were often rewarded with money and privileges when they returned to their home cities.
The ancient Games continued for more than a thousand years, until they were abolished in 393 AD by the Roman emperor, who was a Christian and wanted to end pagan festivals.
The modern Olympics were revived in 1896, in Athens. The driving force behind them was Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator who believed that sport could promote international understanding.
Women first competed in the modern Games in 1900, in a small number of sports such as tennis and golf.
The first Winter Olympics were held in 1924, in Chamonix in France.
Today, one of the biggest challenges facing the Olympics is cost. Many host cities have been left with enormous debts and unused stadiums, and fewer cities are now willing to bid to host the Games.

passages.title: The Race to the Top of the World
paragraphs: For centuries, the highest mountain on Earth was known to the people who lived beneath it by local names: Chomolungma in Tibetan and, later, Sagarmatha in Nepali. Its English name came in 1865, when it was named after George Everest, a British surveyor who had led the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. Everest himself objected, arguing that local names should be used.

Measuring the mountain has proved difficult, because of snow cover and changes caused by earthquakes. In 2020, China and Nepal jointly announced a new official height of 8,848.86 metres, ending a long-running disagreement between the two countries.

The first serious attempts to climb Everest were made by British expeditions in the 1920s. In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine were last seen climbing towards the summit before they disappeared into the clouds. Whether they reached the top before dying remains one of the great mysteries of mountaineering. Mallory's body was finally found in 1999, but it provided no clear answer.

Success came in 1953, with a large British expedition led by John Hunt. On 29 May, Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer from Nepal, reached the summit. They used bottled oxygen, which was essential at a height where the air contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level. News of their success reached London on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

Since then, thousands of people have reached the summit, and climbing Everest has become a major commercial industry. Climbers pay large sums to expedition companies, which provide guides, Sherpa support, equipment and fixed ropes. In 2019, a photograph of a long queue of climbers waiting near the summit shocked the world, and several deaths that season were blamed partly on overcrowding.

The mountain also suffers from serious waste problems. Tonnes of rubbish, from empty oxygen bottles to tents and human waste, have accumulated on the mountain over the decades. The Nepalese government has introduced rules requiring climbers to bring back a certain amount of rubbish, and clean-up campaigns are held regularly, but the problem has not been solved.

passages.title: Powering the Electric Car
paragraphs: Electric cars have moved from the margins to the mainstream remarkably quickly. According to the International Energy Agency, around 18 percent of all new cars sold worldwide in 2023 were electric, compared with just a few percent five years earlier. In some countries, such as Norway, the great majority of new cars are now electric.

At the heart of almost every electric car is a lithium-ion battery. Inside, lithium ions move between two electrodes as the battery charges and discharges. The cost of these batteries has fallen dramatically, by roughly 90 percent since 2010, thanks to improvements in technology and large-scale production. Cheaper batteries have made electric cars far more affordable.

However, the materials used in batteries come at a cost. Much of the world's lithium comes from the so-called 'lithium triangle' of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia, where it is extracted from salty underground water in desert regions. The process uses large amounts of water in some of the driest places on Earth, causing concern among local and indigenous communities. Cobalt, another common battery ingredient, is mined largely in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where investigations have documented dangerous working conditions and child labour.

Partly in response, manufacturers are turning to different battery chemistries. Lithium iron phosphate batteries, which contain no cobalt or nickel, are cheaper and longer-lasting, although they store slightly less energy for their weight. Researchers are also developing sodium-ion batteries, which use sodium, an abundant element found in ordinary salt, instead of lithium.

Recycling offers another solution. Old batteries contain valuable metals, and modern recycling processes can recover up to 95 percent of materials such as lithium, cobalt and nickel. As the number of electric cars grows, recycled materials could supply a significant share of the metals needed for new batteries, reducing the need for mining.

Even when a battery is no longer suitable for a car, it may still have a useful life. Batteries that retain around 70 to 80 percent of their original capacity can be used to store electricity for buildings or for the power grid, helping to balance supply from solar and wind power. This 'second life' could extend a battery's usefulness by many years before it is finally recycled.

passages.title: What Did We Learn From Remote Learning?
paragraphs: In the spring of 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic spread, schools and universities around the world closed their doors. At the peak, UNESCO estimated that more than 1.5 billion students were affected. Almost overnight, teaching moved online, in what has been described as the largest educational experiment in history.

For many children, the results were disappointing. A large analysis of studies from many countries, published in 2023, concluded that students had lost, on average, around a third of a year's learning. Losses were greatest in mathematics and among younger children, who found it hardest to learn independently through a screen. I think it is now clear that, for most children, online learning was not an adequate substitute for the classroom.

The effects were also deeply unequal. Students from wealthier families were more likely to have their own laptop, a reliable internet connection and a quiet place to work, as well as parents who could help them. In poorer households, several children often had to share a single device, or rely on a mobile phone, and many had no internet access at all. As a result, existing gaps in achievement widened.

The experience also revealed how much schools provide beyond academic teaching. For many children, school is where they receive a nutritious meal, meet friends, get help with emotional problems and are noticed by adults if something is wrong at home. When schools closed, these forms of support disappeared, and reports of anxiety and loneliness among young people increased.

Not every lesson was negative. Remote learning worked better for older students who were highly motivated and able to organise their own time. Many universities found that recorded lectures were popular, allowing students to review difficult material or study around jobs and family responsibilities, and most now offer them alongside live teaching. Teachers also became far more confident in using digital tools.

In my view, the main lesson is that technology can support education but cannot replace schools, especially for children. Hybrid approaches, combining online and face-to-face teaching, make sense for universities and adult learners. For younger students, however, the priority should be making sure that schools stay open wherever possible, and governments should invest in helping the students who fell furthest behind to catch up.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the average daily commuting time, in minutes, in five cities in 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the average time people spent commuting each day in Dhaka, Lagos, Tokyo, London and Los Angeles in 2015 and 2025.
Overall, commuting times increased considerably in Dhaka and Lagos, which had the longest journeys in both years, while the figures for the other three cities changed very little.

In 2015, commuters in Dhaka spent the most time travelling, at 70 minutes a day, followed by Lagos at 60 minutes. Tokyo and London had moderate commuting times of 50 and 45 minutes respectively, while Los Angeles had the shortest, at 30 minutes.

By 2025, the average commute in Dhaka had risen by 15 minutes to 85 minutes, and in Lagos it had also increased by 15 minutes, to 75 minutes. In contrast, commuting times fell slightly in Tokyo, to 48 minutes, and in London, to 42 minutes. Los Angeles saw a small rise of two minutes but remained the city with the shortest commute, at 32 minutes.

task2.text: Some people think that plastic bags should be completely banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: Single-use plastic bags have become a symbol of the world's plastic pollution problem, and many countries, including Bangladesh, which banned polythene bags in 2002, have tried to restrict them. I agree that single-use plastic bags should be banned, although I believe the ban must be properly enforced and supported by affordable alternatives.

The environmental case for a ban is strong. Plastic bags are typically used for only a few minutes but can take hundreds of years to break down. Because they are light, they are easily carried by wind and water into rivers and the sea, where they harm wildlife: turtles mistake them for jellyfish, and seabirds become entangled in them. In cities, discarded bags block drains, worsening floods during heavy rain, which was one of the main reasons for Bangladesh's ban.

Opponents argue that bans can cause problems. Some alternatives, such as cotton bags, require far more energy and water to produce, and they only become better for the environment if they are reused many times. Plastic bags are also cheap and convenient, especially for small traders and low-income shoppers. Moreover, the experience of several countries shows that bans are often ignored if they are not enforced.

These objections, however, are reasons to design the ban carefully rather than to reject it. Governments should enforce the law consistently, especially among manufacturers, and encourage cheap, durable alternatives such as jute bags, which also support local industries. Public campaigns can help people get into the habit of carrying reusable bags.
In conclusion, I agree that single-use plastic bags should be banned, but a ban will only succeed if it is enforced and accompanied by practical alternatives.

speaking.cue:
Describe a sporting event you watched or took part in.
You should say:
- what the event was
- where and when it took place
- who you were with
and explain why it was memorable.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a cricket match I watched at the Sher-e-Bangla stadium in Dhaka a few years ago, between Bangladesh and India. I went with my cousins, and getting tickets was a real challenge. We queued for hours outside the ticket office the day before. The atmosphere inside the stadium was incredible. Almost everyone was wearing green and red, people were waving flags and painting their faces, and the noise every time a Bangladeshi player hit a boundary was deafening. The match itself was very close. India batted first and scored quite a lot of runs, so for most of the second half we were nervous. Then two of our batsmen built a long partnership, and the crowd became more and more excited. In the end, Bangladesh won with just a few balls remaining. What made it so memorable was the shared emotion. Thousands of strangers were hugging each other and singing. I'm not usually someone who gets very excited about sport, but that evening I was shouting along with everyone else. It made me understand why sport means so much to people. It brings everyone together, regardless of who they are.
